comments.content:
wasabicards seems interesting. It would be nice to try their real dashboard for some time without paying fee if possible.
I see they mostly tweet in Chinese and all the videos I can find to learn more about them were in Chinese. So, that is probably their main language. Just hoping we don't get API responses in Chinese. 
I see it is same team behind wasabi wallet, so appears to be crypto friendly. 
Also, wasabicards offers only payment cards and not other gift cards and this is probably another plus for our use case. My assumption is that the Reloadly has other revenue generating options like topups and gift cards and that is why they are ok with ignoring payment cards.
I have request access to this doc. It is same email I have already given you in telegram for check-ins.

### Feasibility of wasabicard 
Please note that some info below is based on my previous experience with payment cards and not exactly info provided by wasabicard. wasabicard will reveal much of the info in their contract or after the contract. This feasibility report mostly compares wasabicard to our existing payment card solution. 
Previously we had integrated Reloadly cards. Those were non-reloadable cards. One advantage of these cards was management. We place an order with Reloadly, user gets a card. We almost never store anything. After the card order, we are done. There were separate services offering extra support for redeeming, transactions history, etc. It was not our responsibility.
All cards by wasabicard are reloadable cards. Users will buy them to use for years. It introduces new challenges and complexities in the payment card system.
From starting a contract with wasabi, it affects cardPrice that each user must pay for a new card. There would be other such fees depending on our contract. Please pay close attention to these factors in our contract with wasabi. It depends on our contract if user pays 0$ cardPrice when getting a new card, or 100$. Less is of course better.
As users will use wasabicards for years, we will have to provide them with features and continuous support to deal with
- recharge
- their cards security
- card replacements
- risk rules
- transaction details
- 3D transaction support
- Users can move funds to/from these cards between crypto. So not only UUSD => wasabicard, but also wasabicard => UUSD
- they also have some physical cards, dealing with its shipping/replacement, or at least show shipping info
- contract renew every year. We probably get hit with high fees if we don't bring in high volume. 
- (optional) branding some virtual cards as "UbiquityCard" with extra fee of 100k$. 
A part of me also thinks that wasabicard is too much for us. It is not just a mode of delivering UbiquityOS payment to users, but more like adding a standalone payment product "UbiquityCard". But I also understand that it is a part of vision and goal of this issue specs. 
We will have to develop this product mostly from scratch. We wouldn't be able to reuse much of our existing payment card feature.
I have studied but didn't try their sandbox API. If you want me to try it, give me more time. As the fee by wasabi cards has turned into monthly, we can just try their production API.
We will try to start with the minimum usable product and expand from there. 
If we are okay with the above points and wasabicard monthly/annual fees, I think we can proceed. The next important thing is to get a contract with minimum fees (cardPrice, any monthly, annual, usage fees) and maximum global support.

comments.content:
@minhyeong112 
Do you have a link to their API? I couldn't find any at https://wasabicard.com/.

Overall looks good. As far as I understand those are corporate virtual cards, it means we'll have to maintain a backend to [authorize](https://wasabicard.gitbook.io/wasabicard-api/en/basic/bank-card/card-management#card-auth-transaction) contributors' transactions from those cards. As a side note there're [tons](https://wasabicard.gitbook.io/wasabicard-api/en/basic/bank-card/cardholder-management#cardholder-create) of required personal info fields (email, phone, etc...) on creating a new cardholder (i.e. contributor account) which fits with KYC [task](https://github.com/ubiquity-os/plugins-wishlist/issues/24). I suppose the next step is to purchase a real card, add it to google/apple wallet and try to use it in South Korea.

We should understand that the main wasabi cards use case is **intra company payments**. So its pretty convenient for the following use cases:
- you have an online marketing company and want to fund a card for your marketing employee to spend it **only** on Facebook/Instagram ads 
- you have a taxi park and want to give your drivers a card which can only be spend **only** on gas stations
For our use case wasabi cards are not really scalable, managing cards for 1k of contributors (in terms of backend) is pretty time intensive.
Another pain point (mentioned in telegram chat with wasabi) is that many of the merchants are not supported and should you try to authorize a payment with an unsupported merchant the card will be blocked immediately.
Wasabi cards are good enough for a demo kick start (supporting let's say 100 contributors) but in the end we'll have to leave them because of scalability and their fees.

More brainstorming
We could move from the "mint ubiquity card" approach to "transform your existing bank card to ubiquity card" utilizing CEX withdrawals. We could maintain a single centralized exchange account (for example in https://www.kraken.com/ if their API supports that) and add contributors' cards as withdrawal options.
How it could work:
1. Contributor solves a task and opens `pay.ubq.fi`
2. Contributor selects "cash out to ubiquity card"
3. Contributor inputs his bank card details and `pay.ubq.fi` backend assigns that card to a contributor's ubiquity account
4. `pay.ubq.fi` backend adds that bank card as a withdrawal option in a CEX
5. `pay.ubq.fi` backend initiates a withdrawal request from our own account in a CEX to a contributor's bank card
This way we basically utilize CEX infrastructure for payouts. Of course this is against any CEX rules, not really scalable and I suppose it would be hard to find CEX with API for adding withdrawal methods without strict KYC (like attaching your photo with a bank card) but there are no fees (except for CEX withdrawal fees), all merchants and most of the countries are supported (since the real bank card is used).
This approach solves the task of "getting enough product traction until we find a suitable virtual cards provider".

https://www.reloadly.com has some drawbacks:
1. Upper limit of a single virtual gift card (1000 USD)
2. Not scalable in terms that if we want a single contributor to have a single virtual card (and brand it as "ubiquity card") then right now we have to mint a dozens of gift cards instead of a single virtual bank card.
We should find a proper virtual cards provider with the following features (available via API):
1. Create a virtual card for a contributor
2. Top up a virtual card of a contributor
3. Check virtual card balance
4. Virtual cards must be tokenized (i.e. can be added to Apple/Google wallet) 
5. Virtual cards can be used in South Korea, USA and EU countries
I've sent a couple of inquiries:
| Service  | Status |
| ------------- | ------------- |
| https://www.ininal.com  | Asked for details  |
| https://apibank.club  | Asked for details, doesn't support South Korea  |
| https://wanttopay.net  | No reply  |
| https://pst.net  | Asked for details, doesn't support Apple/Google wallets  |
### January 2025 Addendum
It seems that we are having reliability concerns with reloadly. 
As long as we can find a partner with no monthly fees then it can serve well for our early testing and research of the Ubiquity card program. 
Deliverable should be something similar to the "solution costs" section of our [2023 report](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1m3fcKkPg7aIhkLD0vfJxTZFwGBUdq1vv6UhL2Jt9gcc/edit?usp=sharing). Basically find out pricing and terms for similar providers.
